items.description_text: Humour is already present in youth work practice - but it's rarely used as a deliberate, structured tool. "Humour is Serious Business" (HiSB) is a 6-day Erasmus+ KA153-YOU training course (27 November - 3 December 2026, Hollókő, Hungary) that will help you turn something you probably already do instinctively into an intentional, ethical, and effective competence for engaging young people. This training is aimed specifically at practitioners in the field of non-formal learning and youth work - not at the general public. You should apply if you are a youth worker (professional or voluntary), a youth leader, a young person (18+) with leadership potential already identified by your organisation, or a practitioner with relevant expertise who works with young people (e.g. a coach, mentor or tutor), even if youth work is not your primary profession. Through non-formal methods - World Café, simulations and role play, clowning and improvisation, team building, and daily reflection groups - you will explore the many different types of humour, examine cultural differences in how humour is used, reflect on your own sense of humour, and develop concrete post-programme actions to bring back to your own community. Every participant leaves with a Personal Development Plan and the chance to earn a Youthpass. HiSB is delivered by an experienced international Training Team and hosted by MAVISZ (Hungary), together with partner organisations in Poland, Portugal, Armenia, Serbia, Latvia, Croatia, Montenegro and Spain. 36 participants will take part, 4 per sending country. Full details, including the daily programme, participant support structure, and reimbursement process, are in the Info Pack: https://mavisz.my.canva.site/hisb2026

items.description_text: Across Europe and Neighbouring countries, youth work is increasingly shaped by complex emotional, social and psychological realities. Young people are navigating uncertainty, rapid social change, digital pressure, polarization and declining motivation in education, while youth workers are expected to respond with empathy, stability and inclusive support to these situations. Alongside emotional distress, many youth workers report growing levels of low motivation, disengagement, apathy and lack of initiative among young people, which directly affects participation in learning, community life and democratic processes. However, the emotional demands placed on youth workers are rising faster than the availability of structured training that equips them to manage emotions, both their own and those of the young people they work with, in a healthy, professional and sustainable way. In this context, emotional intelligence is no longer an optional “soft skill,” but a core competence for high-quality youth work, wellbeing promotion, motivation, participation and democratic engagement. "E-motion: A Practical Guide to Emotional Intelligence in Youth Work" training course is designed to respond to this gap by strengthening youth workers’ emotional intelligence as a key professional competence. While youth work is fundamentally based on human relationships, emotional intelligence competences such as self-awareness, emotional regulation, empathy, motivation and constructive communication are often insufficiently addressed within existing non-formal education training pathways. Youth workers frequently lack practical tools to respond to emotional withdrawal, low self-confidence, reduced intrinsic motivation and fear of failure, especially among young people with fewer opportunities. items.description_text: Connected Youth Work: From Non-Formal to Digital is an Erasmus+ international training course for youth workers, trainers, educators, facilitators, youth leaders and NGO representatives who are actively involved in non-formal learning and youth work. The activity is designed for people who want to strengthen their digital and methodological competences and learn how to combine non-formal education with modern digital tools. The programme will explore practical approaches such as storytelling, gamification, project-based learning, visual communication, multimedia creation and interactive online methods, together with the use of digital platforms and AI-supported tools. The training will focus on how digital tools can support, rather than replace, meaningful youth work. Participants will work on designing engaging, inclusive and participatory learning activities that can be used in face-to-face, online and hybrid settings. The course will be highly practical and based on non-formal education. Participants will learn through workshops, group work, peer learning, reflection, experimentation and hands-on creation of digital educational resources. They will also have the opportunity to exchange practices with colleagues from different European countries and develop materials that can later be adapted and used in their own organisations and local communities. The activity is particularly relevant for applicants who already work with young people in NGOs, youth organisations, community initiatives, educational projects or other non-formal learning environments and who are interested in improving the quality, inclusiveness and digital dimension of their youth work.

It focuses especially on supporting young people with fewer opportunities and highly vulnerable youth. Over 7 days, participants will: understand safeguarding and risk management principles in short-term mobilities; explore the personal struggles young people may face abroad (homesickness, communication and language barriers, overwhelm, exclusion) and how to support them; practice first response to distress, conflict resolution and trauma-informed approaches; exchange practices and co-create the Safe Moves Toolkit on Safeguarding in International Youth Mobilities; reflect on competences through Youthpass and the YOCOMO self-assessment. Methods: non-formal education, including simulations, role-plays, case studies, discussions, creative activities and daily reflection groups. The Training Course builds on the results of the project's Study Visit. There, staff from partner organisations observed safeguarding practices in an ESC Team with highly vulnerable young people.

During the training, participants will explore how to recognise signs of emotional distress, communicate supportively, build trust and create a safe environment for young people. The training will also focus on creative and artistic methods that can help young people express emotions, as well as on understanding professional roles and boundaries and recognising when additional professional support may be needed. Key benefits for participants Participants will: deepen their understanding of mental health and emotions in young people; strengthen their ability to recognise signs of emotional distress and crisis; gain practical methods for supporting young people experiencing emotional difficulties; develop tools for building trust and open communication; explore creative and artistic methods for emotional expression; strengthen their understanding of professional boundaries in youth work; exchange practices and experiences with professionals from different countries. Learning approach The training is based on non-formal and experiential learning, combining: interactive workshops and group discussions; practical exercises and case-based activities; creative and artistic methods; reflection and peer learning; facilitation and group work; international exchange of practices and experiences. items.description_text: The EU Youth Conference during the Lithuanian Presidency will take place from 8 to 11 March 2027 in Vilnius. The conference is an integral part of the consultation, bringing together young people from across Europe and EU candidate countries to discuss how to implement Youth Goal #4 at the European level. For two and a half days, delegations of young people and policymakers from more than 40 countries will work together to develop evidence-based recommendations for youth policymakers. This interactive online webinar explores the last of the core polarity pairs of the Polarities of Democracy framework, developed by Dr. William Benet. The session will focus on the relationship between participation & representation, examining why both are essential for democratic societies and how balancing these values can strengthen democratic institutions, participation, and decision-making. The webinar will be led by Ralitsa Rumenova, Fellow of The Institute for the Polarities of Democracy, who will introduce participants to the theoretical foundations of this polarity while encouraging dialogue, critical reflection, and the exchange of experiences. The activity is designed for youth workers, youth leaders, trainers, educators, facilitators, civil society representatives, and other professionals working in the field of non-formal learning and youth work, as well as anyone interested in democracy, civic participation, and social change. Using interactive methods, discussion, and practical examples, participants will: explore the concepts of justice and due process within democratic systems; reflect on current democratic challenges from the perspective of polarity thinking; exchange experiences with participants from different countries and professional backgrounds; discover how the Polarities of Democracy framework can be applied in youth work, non-formal education, and community engagement. The webinar is open to participants from all countries, and no previous knowledge of the Polarities of Democracy framework is required. The event will take place on 27 October 2026 at 19 CET.

items.description_text: About the Training Course What if creating a truly inclusive environment was less about complex theories and more about practical, everyday actions? Action for Inclusion is a training course focused on providing you with new strategies and resources to improve inclusiveness in youth work. Throughout the week, participants will explore the different variables that can become hidden barriers to participation and, most importantly, discover how to dismantle them. The main goal is not just to talk about diversity. It is to discover how to actively build safe spaces, support mental health and manage sensitive realities within our communities. The training will give participants the opportunity to practice these strategies and develop the confidence to address discrimination and incorporate inclusive tools directly into their own educational and youth work activities. What will you get from the Training? You will have the chance to: - Deepen your understanding of what really means to be inclusive in our daily lives. - Acquire practical resources to design and implement inclusive strategies in your working environment. - Create safe spaces with a transversal perspective of the people you’re working with. - Manage sensitive topics confidently within your organisations and communities. - Develop the trust and competences needed to identify and address the discrimination towards different groups. - Face the challenges related with mental health and other obstacles against inclusion in your youth work practices. - Create new international connections and opportunities for cooperation Two experienced facilitators The training will be delivered by Víctor Paterna and Santiago Gallego, two experienced trainers and workers from the NGO sector. Join our 7-day Erasmus+ training course designed to equip you with the essential skills, tools, and confidence to design engaging workshops, understand non-formal learning, and kickstart your project organizer journey. Through intensive days filled with practical methods, dynamic activities, and peer exchange, you will explore group dynamics, practice debriefing, and discover how to handle challenging moments in a group. This training course connects hands-on facilitation to the wider Erasmus+ project lifecycle: from a single 90-minute session to a full international initiative. items.description_text: This webinar explores how youth work can identify barriers to participation, challenge discrimination and use creative methodologies to build more inclusive spaces for young people, drawing from the experience of different NGOs. The session invites youth workers, stakeholders and anyone who might be interested in working with these topics to reflect on the most common challenges found in youth work and to consider concrete ways of designing activities and adapting methodologies/practices to increase access and equal participation. With this purpose in mind, the webinar looks at how arts and creativity can assist with communication and engagement, particularly for those who participate in different ways. Participants will gain practical tools and inspiration to make their own activities more accessible, inclusive and responsive to the diversity of young people.

items.description_text: The world young people navigate today is brittle, anxious, non-linear and incomprehensible. Emotional pressure, digital overload and the psychosocial legacy of the pandemic have turned resilience into a practical competence rather than an abstract quality. Youth workers stand on the front line of this reality, yet they rarely have structured spaces to reflect on their own limits and coping strategies. ANCHOR brings together 24 youth workers from Portugal, France, Spain, Greece, Bulgaria and Malta in Amarante, Northern Portugal. Grounded in non-formal education and the social-ecological model of resilience, the course guides participants from strengthening their own resilience to building tools they can use directly with young people. The programme combines workshops on self-knowledge and emotional regulation, an experiential board game on mental health, nature-based sessions, Theatre of the Oppressed and storytelling, World Café and other participatory methods. Together, participants co-create the ANCHOR Resilience Toolkit (ART), an open educational resource that is tested with students at Escola Secundária de Amarante before participants take it home. Participants will develop competences in: understanding systemic resilience and the BANI world as a basis for youth work emotional self-regulation and burnout prevention through nature-based methods recognising mental health challenges and applying Psychological First Aid within professional boundaries facilitation through gamification, World Café and experiential methods creating psychologically safe spaces through the Safe Space Protocol designing and documenting non-formal education tools as open educational resources The course is part of a wider learning process including preparation (diagnostic questionnaire, learning contract with a mentor, preparatory meeting) and follow-up (local workshops, national online dissemination event, integration of the toolkit into each organisation’s practice). Target group: Youth

items.description_text: The European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC) invites youth workers, youth leaders, trainers, community practitioners and other professionals working in non-formal learning and youth work to join the first session of Equal Ground, a quarterly ENRMSC dialogue series exploring meaningful participation, access to opportunities and accountability. About the session A seat at the table means little if the decisions are already made. Equal Ground Q1: Meaningful Participation — Beyond the Seat at the Table explores what meaningful participation looks like when refugees, migrants, stateless people and other communities are not simply invited into conversations, but have genuine opportunities to influence decisions, policies and actions. The session will examine the difference between being present and participating meaningfully. Who gets invited to the table? Who gets heard? Who gets to influence what happens next? Through a participatory, community-centred dialogue, participants will explore barriers to meaningful participation and consider how youth workers, organisations and institutions can create more effective pathways for people with lived experience to contribute to decision-making. What will participants explore? How can we recognise when a group needs action and when it needs time to pause, process or simply be? items.description_text: The central focus of the exchange is how we can address difficult and polarising topics in youth work and what stance we, as youth workers, should take when dealing with them. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict also has a significant impact on German society. In schools, youth centres and summer camps, youth workers are repeatedly confronted with challenging situations in which young people make derogatory remarks about other groups and show little willingness to engage with different perspectives. Together with a group from Israel, we want to exchange experiences, explore different perspectives and discuss how constructive and meaningful youth work can be sustained, even in challenging times. Antisemitism and anti-Muslim hostility shape the debate surrounding the conflict. Through this project, we aim to equip people who have to navigate the impact of these debates in their everyday professional lives with new methods and approaches, while providing them with space to reflect on their own positions and develop strategies for dealing with challenging situations. Learning Objectives Facilitate challenging dialogue spaces that embrace ambiguity and make room for different perspectives. Through the body, movement, connection and experiences on land and in water, we’ll play with support, boundaries, trust, letting go and the different ways we can stay afloat. We will work through embodiment, breathwork, movement, PlayFight, body awareness and grounding practices, together with structured aquatic methodologies in warm water. We’ll explore trust, support, boundaries, consent, co-regulation and letting go through experiential exercises, both individually and with others. The programme will also include reflection circles, peer learning, group processes and participant-led practice, giving us space not only to experience the methods ourselves, but also to explore how they can be adapted to our work with others. Disclaimer: This program is offered as a learning and training experience. It focuses on practical tools, reflection, and shared exploration. It is not therapy, and it is not intended to replace professional mental health care or clinical support. Embodiment On land, we will work with body awareness, grounding, breath, movement and reflective practices. We will explore how stress shows up in the body, how we can recognise it earlier, and what helps us return to a state where we can respond rather than simply react. items.description_text: In 2023, after 10 years of cultivating participation and reflection around power and decision making , Hors Pistes transformed its governance system into a collective coordination inspired by sociocratic principles. 3 years later, we acknowledge the need of sharing with the outside world the experiences (success and failures) and all the questions that came-up throughout this experiment. With other curious and motivated people working in the youth field we’d like to explore the topics of shared governance and transformation of hierarchical structures. We want to open a space to question the connection between the values of youth work and the real organisations’ internal practices and power dynamics. We want to explore the sparks, the beauty but also the contradictions and limits of this type of system. The course will explore how adventure and experiential learning can help people develop greater self-awareness, confidence, resilience, emotional regulation, connection with others and a stronger sense of personal wellbeing. Participants will have the opportunity to: experience adventure and outdoor experiential learning first-hand; explore the relationship between experience, reflection and personal growth; develop greater awareness of their own resources, limits and learning patterns; understand how nature and adventure can contribute to wellbeing and meaningful learning; explore facilitation and reflective practices that help transform an experience into learning; exchange practices and perspectives with youth workers and educators from different European contexts; reflect on how these approaches can be transferred into their own work with young people. items.title: Life in It Training Course
items.summary: Life in It is a two-part Erasmus+ media training for youth workers and educators, combining practical filmmaking, storytelling and short-form video in Germany and Greece, with local practice between the two phases.
items.participants_countries: Czech Republic, Germany, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Slovak Republic
items.fee_text: There is a 50 euro participation fee per phase of the project.
items.accommodation_food_text: All accommodation and food costs will be covered by the programme.
items.travel_reimbursement_text: For the travel reimbursement, we follow the Erasmus+ Programme guide and the distance calculator. Please refer to the infopack for the exact amount of your country.
items.description_text: Life in It is a two-part Erasmus+ media training for people active in youth work and non-formal learning, including youth workers, trainers, educators, volunteers, project coordinators and people involved in their organisation’s communication. No previous filmmaking experience is required; the focus is on learning through practice, collaboration and experimentation. The learning journey starts with online preparation and continues with Frame One in Germany (13–19 December 2026), where participants explore practical filmmaking, storytelling and media tools by working in international crews and creating content in real local contexts. Between the two international phases, participants bring the learning into their own organisation or community, including a small focus group with young people and further local practice. The journey continues with Frame Two at Hopeland, Greece (22–29 September 2027), where participants explore how the same storytelling foundations can be adapted to shorter, vertical video and social media formats. The methodology is strongly based on non-formal education and learning by doing: short inputs, practical assignments, teamwork, feedback, reflection and creative decision-making are at the centre of the programme. Life in It is designed as one learning journey rather than two separate trainings, with online preparation, two residential phases, local practice and follow-up. Priority is given to applicants who can take part in the complete process and use the learning afterwards in their youth work, organisation or local community.

items.title: Move, Play, Create : Circus and Physical Theatre as Tools for Youth Work
items.summary: A practical training for youth workers to discover circus and theatre as tools for non-formal education, exploring accessible activities that foster creativity, confidence, cooperation and social connection.

items.description_text: This training course introduces youth workers, educators and facilitators to circus and theatre as practical tools for youth work and non-formal education. No previous circus or theatre experience is required. Through hands-on activities, participants will discover the basics of juggling, partner and group acrobatics, clowning and physical theatre, while learning how to adapt these activities into accessible and meaningful workshops for young people. The course is based on circus pedagogy: an educational approach that uses circus not primarily to train performers, but to support personal and social development. Circus activities create opportunities to cooperate, communicate, build trust, take on challenges, be creative and experience success. Participants will explore how these activities can foster young people's confidence, creativity, cooperation, persistence, coordination and social connection. A key focus will be accessibility and inclusion, exploring how circus can be adapted to different ages, physical abilities, levels of experience and backgrounds. Participants will also discover how a group can move from individual games and activities towards creating a short collective performance. They will explore the pedagogical and practical aspects of the creative process, including generating ideas, sharing roles, connecting different disciplines and ensuring that everyone can contribute. By the end of the training, participants will have a practical repertoire of circus and theatre activities and greater confidence in using them in their youth work.

items.description_text: Project Summary: Leveraging ICT and Social Media for Youth Inclusion and Participation Aim of the Project: The project is designed to equip youth workers with digital skills and tools to strengthen civic participation and engage young people through Information and Communication Technology (ICT). A core aim is to promote civic engagement through digital tools. Objectives: Strengthen Digital Competencies: Provide practical training in ICT, social media engagement, and digital content creation. Youth workers will be trained to guide young people in critical media analysis, recognizing misinformation, and using digital platforms for youth activism and community participation. Ensure Inclusion and Equal Access: Develop strategies to engage marginalized and disadvantaged young people who face barriers to digital participation. Encourage Innovation: Introduce interactive, gamified, and blended learning approaches to make digital engagement more dynamic and adaptive. Strengthen Transnational Cooperation: Establish a European Digital Youth Work Network for collaboration and knowledge exchange, and develop a Digital Civic Engagement Toolkit with practical resources. Outcome: The project aims to significantly enhance the digital skills of youth workers and strengthen youth engagement through the use of digital tools for non-formal education and social participation. It seeks to expand civic participation through youth-led activism and make digital youth work more accessible and inclusive for young people from diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. The project's sustainability will be ensured through the creation of a European-wide network of digital youth workers and an open-access toolkit, ensuring that the methodologies remain relevant and scalable.

items.description_text: The ENRMSC European Dialogue & Capacity-Building Forum 2027 will take place in Warsaw, Poland, in April 2027. The forum will bring together young refugees, migrants and stateless changemakers, youth workers, youth leaders, researchers, academics, civil society organisations, public institutions and other practitioners working with young people. The forum is built around a simple question: How can we move from young people being affected by systems to young people meaningfully shaping knowledge, opportunities, policies and solutions? The programme will explore meaningful participation, access to education and professional opportunities, community leadership, research and evidence, youth engagement, advocacy and collaboration between communities and institutions. Participants will take part in interactive discussions, panel sessions, workshops and facilitated group activities. The programme will combine knowledge exchange with practical capacity-building and opportunities for participants to develop new connections and potential European cooperation. A particular focus will be placed on recognising lived experience as expertise. Young refugees, migrants and stateless people will not only participate as beneficiaries but as contributors, knowledge holders, community leaders and partners in shaping discussions and recommendations. The forum will also connect participants with relevant European opportunities, networks and potential partners, including opportunities related to youth work, education, research, leadership and civic participation. The event is particularly relevant to people working in non-formal learning and youth work who engage with young people from refugee, migrant and stateless backgrounds. The guiding principle of the forum is: “Nothing About Us Without Us.” The forum is currently being developed by the European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC), a refugee-, migrant- and stateless-led European civil society organisation.

The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
